name: Prospero Win
description: Windows compatibility runtime for native PlayStation 5 homebrew.
author: mpereiraesaa
release_notes:
prospero-win v0.2.0 is the biggest update since the first release. 32-bit Windows games now run directly on the PS5's CPU instead of through the translator, Vulkan traffic is batched so DXVK games keep their frame rate, OpenGL games draw through Mesa's Zink, and Windows programs can finally reach the internet by name and over HTTPS.

New to prospero-win? The v0.1.0 release notes explain what it is, what you need and how to add your first game.

Highlights
- 32-bit games run natively. No more instruction translation for 32-bit games by default; the translator stays available as a per-game option and as an automatic fallback.
- Vulkan command batching for 32-bit games, so DXVK and Zink games aren't held back by the cost of switching between the game and the system.
- OpenGL through Zink. OpenGL games no longer need a special build of the app; Mesa's Zink ships in the package.
- Online-ready networking. Host names resolve through the console's own resolver, and Windows' TLS (schannel) works, with a pinned set of root certificates.
- Many fixes found while bringing up GTA San Andreas, GTA IV, Counter-Strike 1.6, Atomic Bomberman, Pizza Tower and larger Windows programs.

What's new

32-bit games on the native CPU
Until now, every 32-bit game ran through prospero-win's x86 translator. In v0.2.0 a 32-bit game runs on the console's CPU in 32-bit mode, through a new WoW64 backend (#432). Games run their own code at full speed; only calls into the system cross over.
- Works on any firmware. The native backend needs to register its signal handlers directly with the kernel. It now finds that entry point in libkernel itself instead of relying on one measured firmware build, and checks it before use, including the layout of the kernel's signal frame (#681).
- Automatic fallback. If the native backend can't start on a console for any reason, the game now runs on the translator instead of closing (#677, thanks to leolobato).
- Your choice per game. [runtime] cpu = translator in a game's profile keeps it on the translator. 64-bit games are unaffected; they always ran natively.
- Stable under load. A rare timing window could send a game thread back into 32-bit code with the wrong thread state. It showed up as GTA San Andreas closing about two seconds after start, depending on its shader cache (#683, #682).

Vulkan batching and faster graphics
Each call from a game into the system costs a couple of microseconds on the console, and DXVK makes tens of thousands of Vulkan calls per frame. v0.2.0 queues those calls and sends them over in batches, always in order, and only waits where the game needs an answer (#432 and the batching work before it).
- Counter-Strike 1.6 under Zink went from 2,234 to 24 crossings per frame, with no change in what's drawn, now that descriptor writes are batched too (#672, #674).
- Shader compiles no longer stall other threads. Pipeline compiles run outside the batch lock, so one long compile no longer freezes the render thread (#676).
- A real shader cache. RADV now keeps its compiled shaders between launches, under /data/prospero-win/cache/radv. Before, every launch compiled every pipeline again (#668).
- prospero-win builds of DXVK. Game recipes can pin a tuned DXVK build. DXVK 2.6.2-prospero2 adds cheaper CS-thread work and options used by the GTA San Andreas and GTA IV recipes (#407, #680).

OpenGL games through Zink
OpenGL games now draw through Mesa's Zink on top of Vulkan, on the native CPU with batching. Zink ships inside the app, so OpenGL games work with the regular package; the separate PS5 OpenGL SDK build is gone (#438, #456–#466). Existing profiles with graphics = opengl switch over on their own.

Networking
- Host names resolve. Windows programs could only reach numeric addresses before. Names now go through the console's own resolver, using its network settings, with bounded timeouts and a short cache for failed lookups (#384).
